prize_parts.citation: for foundational contributions to the analysis of nominal rigidities and monetary policy rules: time-dependent price setting, staggered contracts and interest-rate rules, and their integration into a micro-founded framework for monetary policy

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged in substance: B014 with Calvo, Taylor and Woodford. The case rests on three separable, load-bearing contributions. Calvo supplied the tractable pricing friction on which the forward-looking Phillips curve is built. Taylor supplied staggered contracts and a simple, testable policy rule. Woodford combined them into a welfare-based general-equilibrium theory of interest and prices. The work is 25 to 40 years old, is used in both research and central-bank practice, and has been stress-tested by 2008, the zero lower bound and 2021-23. In each episode the response has been to extend the framework, including heterogeneous-agent versions, which keep nominal rigidities and policy rules as components. As Krusell argues, that is evidence of foundational status, though I discount his view somewhat because we are frequent co-authors. In this round I tightened the citation to answer the chair's question on scope. It now says 'foundational contributions' and names the three components, so it does not claim the estimated-DSGE tradition or the whole literature. The estimation and identification work of Christiano, Eichenbaum and Evans, Smets and Wouters, Galí and Gertler can be described in the Scientific Background as related work. Only the prize citation is limited to three names. I recognise this cannot remove the implied cost of exclusion. I still judge B014 ahead of B003 on breadth of influence on scientific practice and policy, durability, and the absence of an earlier prize for this core. I do not rely on how many colleagues prefer it. My alternatives changed: B030 is replaced by B047. That is not because of its support count. The mixed empirical record of Protection for Sale is one reason. The other is that Helpman's strongest credited claim, if the Committee wants a trade award, seems to me to lie with Melitz and the heterogeneous-firm framework. B003 stays my first alternative.
statement.case_against: Attribution remains the main weakness and is not resolved by wording. Galí, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Evans, Gertler, Smets and Wouters have serious claims, and a three-name cap forces a choice that a reader of the field could call arbitrary. The third name (Calvo or Galí) is a judgement call, and Galí's claim is stronger if the Committee weights the empirical framework. There is also a conceptual question whether Calvo's compact pricing device is a discovery of the kind the Committee usually rewards. Boppart's observation is fair: Calvo's and Taylor's older primitives differ in kind from the Woodford and Galí synthesis. Performance in the 2008 crisis and in the post-2021 inflation is contested, and representative-agent versions may be seen as a superseded stage. Earlier macro prizes (rational expectations, time consistency, VAR methods, Bernanke 2022) may narrow the marginal room, though I read them as not covering this core. Finally, B003 has the cleaner attribution, and I should not let my familiarity with the macro literature and with Krusell and Boppart make B014's attribution problem look smaller than it is.

responses.point: Strömberg prefers B003 and says he would support B014 if a defensible narrower citation or attribution were agreed. Without one, he judges B003 the cleaner prize. He also separates Kiyotaki-Moore (borrowers' collateral and asset-price amplification) from the 2022 prize on banks as intermediaries.
responses.response: I take the condition seriously and offer the tightened wording above. It names the pricing friction, the contract and rule, and the micro-founded framework, and says 'foundational'. It avoids the claim to cover the estimated tradition or the field as a whole. I accept that this limits the claim but does not remove the cost of exclusion. I also concede your 2022 point. Your distinction between borrower collateral and bank intermediation persuades me that the overlap is smaller than I implied in round 1. My ordering of B014 over B003 therefore rests on breadth of influence on practice and on the absence of any earlier prize for the pricing and rule core. It does not rest on B003 being crowded out. If the Committee weights attribution clarity above breadth, B003 is a defensible prize, and I keep it as my first alternative.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson keeps Calvo over Galí because Calvo's pricing mechanism is the primitive of the New Keynesian Phillips curve, but she would not object strongly to Galí in place of Calvo if the Committee weights empirical validation and the estimated-model tradition more heavily. She also notes that the original Kiyotaki-Moore contribution has thin direct empirical identification.
responses.response: We agree on the structure of the choice. The swap depends on what the citation rewards. If it rewards the mechanisms and the rule, Calvo is the originator. If it rewards the empirical, estimated framework, Galí's claim rises, but then Christiano, Eichenbaum and Evans and Smets and Wouters also come into play and three names cannot cover that. That is why I keep the citation on foundations and Calvo in the trio, rather than half-crediting an estimation tradition. I remain open to Galí if the Committee reads the prize differently, and I record that as a real uncertainty. I also agree with you on B003's identification, but I count it as a modest point against B003. The mechanism's later quantitative support is substantial.

responses.point: Boppart prefers B047 and ranks B014 second. He says the framework is fully mature but that any trio is contestable on attribution, because Calvo's and Taylor's older contract and rule insights differ from Woodford's and Galí's modern synthesis. The Committee therefore has to say which layer it is crediting. He sees B047 as having the cleaner attribution.
responses.response: That is the right question, and the revised citation answers it. The prize credits the foundational layer: the pricing friction, the contract and rule, and the normative synthesis. It does not credit the estimated layer. I agree this is a choice and not a neutral description. I accept that B047 has a tighter attribution, and I said so in round 1. But I think the priority questions (Bernard, Eaton, Jensen, Kortum, Hopenhayn) and the 2008 overlap make B047's citation harder to draft than you suggest. Also, as you stressed, timing is not merit, so the absence of a trade prize since 2008 should not count for it. I keep B047 as an alternative, and I do not rank it below B003 on scientific grounds.

responses.point: Andersson moved to the Calvo, Taylor and Woodford trio but argues that Christiano, Eichenbaum and Evans are not merely derivative: identifying monetary shocks and estimating a medium-scale model is a different kind of contribution that a mechanisms-and-rules citation does not capture. He calls this a real cost of the cap. He keeps B006 only as an alternative.
responses.response: I agree, and it shapes the wording. The Christiano-Eichenbaum-Evans work answers a different question (how to identify monetary shocks and make the model usable), so I do not call it a development of the trio. The citation should not suggest that it is. The honest position is that the prize would credit one achievement, the foundations, and the estimation and identification strand is a second achievement that three names cannot hold. I do not think this makes the attribution unresolvable, but it does mean the citation should be narrow. On B006, your acknowledgement that recent game-theory prizes weigh on the marginal case is consistent with my own reasoning. I would ask you to treat B014's attribution cost with the same candour you apply to your own favourite.

responses.point: Teorell prefers the Kiyotaki-Moore pair for B003. He reads the 2022 prize as a different mechanism (banks and intermediation) and says the overlap is a matter of citation drafting. He keeps B014 as his first alternative and says his hesitation is attribution, plus the post-2021 inflation and representative-agent questions about what is being rewarded.
responses.response: I accept your drafting point about B003, and it pushes me to concede that my round-1 overlap worry was overstated. On your B014 hesitation, I agree attribution is the real cost and I have not claimed to solve it. I would read the post-2021 evidence as follows. The specific observation that would count against the foundations is a finding that nominal rigidities and policy rules are no longer needed to explain how monetary policy affects the economy. I know of no such finding in the supplied discussion, and Krusell's account is that heterogeneous-agent models retain these components. That supports reading the episode as an extension. I cannot verify this independently, and a member who reads the evidence the other way should state the specific observation.

uncertainties: Whether the third B014 name should be Calvo or Galí, and whether the Committee prefers a citation weighted toward the empirical and estimated framework. In that case the three-name cap would force an unfair exclusion of Christiano, Eichenbaum, Evans, Smets and Wouters.
Whether the 'foundational contributions' wording is accepted as not implying a ranking of the omitted contributors, or whether the cap makes the attribution problem unresolvable.

How much weight to give the post-2021 inflation episode and the heterogeneous-agent critique when judging maturity. I read them as extensions but cannot settle the question from the supplied evidence.

How to apply a consistent standard to prior-prize overlap across B003 (2022), B032 (2024), B047 and B030 (2008) and B006 (2005-2020), and whether B014's claim that no earlier prize covered the pricing and rule core would survive close examination.
Priority and attribution rest on my background knowledge of the literature. I have not independently verified them, and none of the supplied evidence does so.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure. From my profile, no co-authorship or institutional link to Calvo, Taylor, Woodford, Kiyotaki, Moore, Melitz or Helpman is apparent. I disclose co-authorship with committee colleagues Per Krusell (secretary), Timo Boppart and Richard Friberg, and IIES colleagueship with Krusell and Boppart. Krusell proposes the same B014 trio, so I have tried not to treat his agreement as evidence of merit. As chair I am counted among the six explicit B014 preferences in the round-1 summary, and several of the other supporters have disclosed ties to me. I flag this as a reason to weigh my vote with the arguments and not the count. My own research on climate-economy models, dynamic public finance and quantitative macro is adjacent to the New Keynesian tradition in method, which could produce a familiarity bias. In 2018 I gave the presentation speech, and the 2018 background cites my own work. Neither is connected to a shortlisted candidate. My profile does not state Persson's affiliation, but IIES is associated with political economics, so a possible institutional connection to B032 should be noted. B032 is not in my configuration. Conflicts are disclosed, not adjudicated.
